nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist and writer of the domestic and historical tale of New England, the most considerable American woman fiction-writer of the 1820s and 1830s and a chief practitioner of the Protestant moral tale
literary_identity: A writer of prose fiction, chiefly domestic, moral and historical novels and shorter tales, together with a body of religious and educational narrative, a memoir of a friend and occasional biographical and editorial work. She published her first two novels without her own name and wrote in the manner of the novel of character and conscience rather than of romance or sensation.
biography: She was born at Stockbridge, Massachusetts, on 28 December 1789, the daughter of Theodore Sedgwick, a Federalist member of Congress from Massachusetts and later chief justice of the state, and of Pamela Dwight Sedgwick of the Stockbridge Dwight family. She grew up in the Stockbridge household, where a woman formerly held in slavery who had obtained her freedom by suit in the courts of the state served the family, and an early religious experience attached her to the Unitarian sympathy rather than to the strict Calvinism of her parents' world. Her own illness and convalescence in 1816, when she was nursed by a physician of the new school and read the novels she had been forbidden, decided her upon fiction as her work. A New-England Tale appeared anonymously in 1822, Redwood followed in the same concealment in 1824, and with Hope Leslie in 1827 her name first stood upon a title-page and her reputation as a writer of the national tale was made. Through the 1830s she published tales of New England and of colonial history, wrote for the annuals and for her friend's magazine, and supported her family by her pen; Elm Park, the Stockbridge house, became her home and a centre of the country's literary visiting. She remained unmarried by choice, corresponded widely with the men of letters of her generation, and after her brother's death wrote a memoir and an account of the household which had formed her. She died in 1867 at the age of seventy-seven, and by the end of her life was beginning to be read as the representative woman novelist of the early republic.
literary_profile: Her novels fall into a domestic and moral group, treating conscience, prejudice and the discipline of a young woman's judgment, and a historical group, treating the colonial and Indian border of New England; between them are shorter tales, religious and educational narratives and contributions to the literary annuals. Her habit is the novel of opinion and character, argued through a heroine's errors of judgment, with the sect, the party and the treatment of the Indian brought into the moral account. The memoir and the family narrative show the same concern with testimony, character and the reliability of a community's memory.
stylistic_characteristics: A clear, straightforward and consciously unadorned narrative prose, with a firm control of the middle-length sentence and an economy of description; her force lies in the analysis of motive and in the dialogue of household and country society. She is careful of probability, dislikes the machinery of sensation, and closes her argument with a moral reckoning which she declines to dress up as providence.
intellectual_concerns: The duty and the right of private judgment against priest, party and neighbour; the education of a woman's mind and the claims of an unmarried woman's independence; the treatment of the Indian and the justice of the settlement; sectarian bitterness and the possibility of a reasonable religion; slavery, freedom and the memory of service in the household; the authority of prejudice in a small community; the obligations of the powerful to the dependent.
historical_significance: She established the woman's American novel on grounds of conscience and social argument rather than sentiment, and Hope Leslie gave the colonial and Indian material a critical treatment unmatched before her. For half a century she was the example by which the professional woman fiction-writer of the republic was understood, and recent scholarship has returned her to the history of the American novel and of the argument over removal.
major_influences: Her father's Federalist public life and the Stockbridge country
the English moral novel and the tale of character
the New England colonial chronicles and the histories of the Massachusetts settlements
the Unitarian preaching of reason and duty
the example of the Scottish and English writers of the national historical tale
the annuals and the London magazines for which she wrote
biographical_uncertainty: Accounts differ as to the place of her death, some putting it at Stockbridge and others at a relative's house in the neighbourhood of Boston; the exact share of the physician who superintended her convalescence in determining her career rests chiefly on her own autobiographical papers.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist, tale-writer and editor of the early republic, working in Philadelphia and New York; the first American writer of prose fiction to attempt a professional literary career
literary_identity: A writer of prose fiction and of periodical and editorial work: four gothic narratives published in 1798 and 1799, a domestic romance of 1801, tales and sketches for the magazines he edited, and moral, political and historical argument in essays, prefaces and reviews. He wrote no verse of consequence and no drama; his criticism lives in advertisements and periodical matter rather than in a treatise.
biography: He was born in Philadelphia on 7 January 1771, the son of Elijah Brown, a Quaker merchant of English descent, and grew up within the discipline of the Society of Friends. The prosperity of his father's house broke up in the early 1790s, and the loss of a commercial fortune of his own while still in his twenties decided him upon the pen. He had already left the Friends after a religious crisis of opinion, and turned instead to the rational dissent he found in Godwin and in the English moralists. In 1796 he began Brown's Weekly Political Intelligencer and in 1797 the American Monthly Magazine, the first of several editorial ventures by which he tried to live by periodical writing in the United States. During 1798 and 1799 the Philadelphia publisher Mathew Carey issued his four novels in quick succession, and their reception, hostile at home and warmer in Britain, encouraged him to believe that an American romance of ideas was possible. He tried briefly and unsuccessfully to practise law after being admitted to practice, and for a season kept a country place in the New Jersey shore and in the Genesee region with no better result. From 1806 to 1811 he edited The American Register at New York and Philadelphia, a miscellany which reprinted British review criticism and American news and gave him the largest reading public he ever commanded. He died in Philadelphia in 1810, at the age of thirty-nine, leaving editorial and historical projects unfinished.
literary_profile: His fiction divides into the four gothic narratives of 1798 and 1799 and the later domestic romance of 1801, with tales and sketches scattered through the magazines he controlled. His non-fictional work is larger than his surviving novels and consists of prefaces, reviews, political intelligence, historical and biographical compilation and editorial matter of every kind. The whole of it is prose, and its most distinctive feature is the argumentative narrative: a plot of evidence, rumour and mistaken testimony carried by speakers who reason about their own case. He also wrote on the abolition of slavery and on the condition of the Indian countries, and his western tale draws upon captive narratives as well as upon romance.
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, unadorned and deliberately rational diction applied to scenes of terror; long first-person confessions, letters within letters, and a preference for memoir and journal forms over the plot of the ordinary romance. Explanation is pushed so hard that it becomes an engine of doubt, and the tales end in contentions about what the evidence proves. Topographical and medical detail is used to give the marvellous an air of report, and the prefaces argue the moral purpose of the fiction before the fiction is allowed to speak.
intellectual_concerns: Godwinian inquiry into the power of opinion over conduct; enthusiasm as a disease of the imagination and its relation to religious and political credulity; the pathology of solitude and sleep; the credibility of testimony and the limits of evidence; the condition of women without fortune or protection; slavery, manumission and the meaning of republican equality; the interior frontier as a moral as well as a geographical zone; the education of a republic and the uses of periodical literature.
historical_significance: He created the American gothic and with it the first American prose fiction taken seriously by British reviewers, so that the history of the American novel cannot be written beginning anywhere else. His treatment of belief, sleep and pursued virtue opened lines of development that run through later American romance, and his editorial labours showed what a man of letters in the republic could actually do for a living. Twentieth-century scholarship, which at first set him aside as an oddity, restored the four novels to the canonical history of gothic and early American fiction.
major_influences: William Godwin's Political Justice and Caleb Williams
the epistolary novel of Richardson
Ann Radcliffe and the romance of terror
Quaker autobiographical and examining practice
the yellow-fever narratives of Philadelphia in 1793 and 1798
captive and Indian-tradition narratives of the Pennsylvania and western country
Condillac and the Scottish philosophy of the human mind
the British review criticism which he reprinted
biographical_uncertainty: The chronology of his legal studies and his admission to practice is imperfectly settled; the religious crisis which ended his connection with the Friends is known only from his own allusions and from those of his family; and the cause of his death at thirty-nine, variously reported as consumption and as an acute fever, cannot be determined from the surviving accounts.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist, romancer of forest and sea, satirist of society and naval historian, the first American writer of prose fiction to sustain a European reputation as a creator of a national romance
literary_identity: A novelist above all, and the founder of the American romance of the frontier and of the sea; he also wrote travel and social criticism, a naval history and a body of controversial prefatory and political prose. His fiction divides into the historical and Indian tales, the sea tales, the settlement and frontier tales and the later domestic and political romances; he wrote no verse of consequence.
biography: He was born at Burlington, New Jersey, on 15 September 1789, the son of William Cooper, a member of the legislature who laid out the village of Cooperstown in the Otsego country, and he was bred from infancy in that new settlement on the edge of the western wilderness. Sent to Yale at thirteen, he withdrew without taking a degree and was placed in the merchant service, from which he passed into the navy as a midshipman, serving in the years before and during the war with Great Britain and resigning in 1811 on the eve of his marriage. He settled in the country of his youth, lived for a season in St. Louis territory and in Washington, and turned to fiction after a chance comparison with a popular English romance. Precaution appeared in 1820 and The Spy in 1821, and the frontier tales of the 1820s, ending with The Prairie of 1827, established his fame. From 1826 to 1833 he lived abroad chiefly in Paris and Italy, with a brief appointment as consul at Algiers which he did not use, and during those years wrote the sea romances, the Italian and Dutch historical tales and the travel book Notions of the Americans. His return brought a long quarrel with the American press and with the society he found waiting for him, and in his last decade he answered his critics in fiction, in political argument and in the history of the American navy. He died at his home in Cooperstown on 14 September 1851.
literary_profile: His career may be read as a series of groups: the society and historical tales of 1820 to 1823, the Indian and frontier romance of the Ottsego stories and the Prairie, the sea tales of the late 1820s, the Italian and European romances of the 1830s, and the home criticism of the last ten years. He is the only American writer of his generation whose work holds both the maritime and the wilderness subject at the same scale, and he prefaced and defended his own theory of romance in a large body of prefaces, letters and polemical pamphlets. The naval history and the travel books stand beside the fiction as deliberate contributions to the national record and to the argument about American institutions.
stylistic_characteristics: A vigorous, spacious and often unequal narrative prose, capable of sustained description of forest, coast and sea and of an impressive rhetorical elevation in the speech of his chief personages. He uses the surveyor's eye and the chronicler's manner, interpolates document, ballad and legend, and lets his narrators moralise at length; dialogue is often stately and repetitive, and his satire of society is carried by a frank and indignant declamation rather than by irony.
intellectual_concerns: The wilderness as the moral scene of the republic and the fate of its original possessors; the relation of genuine to borrowed rank and of merit to privilege; the abuses of a corrupted press and of a party-democracy; the justifiable order of a settled community; the sea service as a school of heroism and of national character; the romance of the frontier, the capture, the scout and the boundary between civilisation and the wild; the Christian and republican answer to aristocratic travel.
historical_significance: He made the American frontier and the American sea service subjects of serious romance, and the Leather-stocking series gave the national literature its first continuous mythical cycle. His contemporaries in Europe read and imitated him, and his sea tales founded the tradition of American maritime fiction. At the same time his treatment of Indian removal and of the displaced possessor of the soil became the central instance in the later argument about what the American romance had been willing to see.
major_influences: Scott's Waverley romances and their machinery of historical fiction
the frontier captivity and scout narratives of the New York and Pennsylvania border
his own eight years in the navy and the merchant service
the sea journals and the classical romance of Marryat and of the older voyagers
the fashionable society novel of the English annuals
the Dutch and Indian traditions of the Otsego country as told by his father's neighbours
the political debate of the Whig and Democratic parties of New York
biographical_uncertainty: The story of the wager or chance comparison that first set him to write a novel is anecdotal and variously told; the dating of some of the sea tales' composition rests on letters and on his own later statements rather than on manuscripts.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; essayist, tale-writer, poet of the frontier, dramatist and office-holder, the partner of Irving in the periodical that founded the Knickerbocker group and a defender of a plain native literature
literary_identity: A writer of periodical papers, character sketches, domestic and frontier tales, a poem of the backwoodsman's argument and a play of native comedy, joined to a long after-life in office and in public letter. His work is the democratic and contentious side of the New York school, and he wrote verse, prose fiction and drama without settling on either.
biography: He was born in New York City on 22 August 1778 into a family of Dutch and English descent long settled about the Hudson, and he grew up in the country which supplied the legend of his later tales. He was a friend of Irving from boyhood and with him and a brother conducted in 1807 and 1808 the periodical papers which gave the American essay its first native school. He tried law and a commercial life in New York and in the southern cities without success, and after his return wrote The Backwoodsman, a two-canto argument for the western settler and against borrowed European taste, which appeared in 1818. In the same season he published a play of New York character and a volume of tales and sketches, and from the papers and sketches of these years the Dutchman's Fireside of 1831 was finally drawn. He held federal office in the 1830s and was Secretary of the Navy from 1838 to 1840, an appointment which ended his literary career in everything but pamphlet and preface. He retired to the family place at Fishkill on the Hudson, where he died on 6 April 1860.
literary_profile: His work is a mixture of the periodical essay, the descriptive poem of argument, the frontier and Hudson valley tale, and a comedy of native character; it is continuous in one design, the assertion of American plainness against aristocratic and foreign pretension. He is the least finished and most outspoken of the Knickerbocker writers, and his tales of the Dutch country and of the western settlement supplied material and argument which his friend's sketches did not touch.
stylistic_characteristics: A blunt, polemical and homely prose, strongly accented, given to direct address and to invective against rank, and carrying the argument of the piece on its sleeve. His verse is in the descriptive and argumentative couplet of the earlier American school, robust and unpolished, and his character drawing proceeds by the outside stroke of custom and speech rather than by analysis.
intellectual_concerns: The republican objection to hereditary wealth and to the borrowed standards of Europe; the merits of the backwoods settler and of plain democratic character; the Dutch settlement of the Hudson valley as a vanished society; the claims of a native literature and of native subject; the corruption of office and of party in the republic; the hospitality, superstition and quietly treated custom of the old country.
historical_significance: As the joint author of the first Knickerbocker periodical he shares the founding of the American sketch and character tale, and his poem of 1818 is the earliest considerable statement of the claim to a national literature in American verse. His Dutch tale preserved one version of the Hudson valley legend on which later writing about the region drew, and his contentious defence of democratic plainness marks the political edge of the New York school.
major_influences: The Addison and Goldsmith manner of the periodical essay as read in New York
the Dutch and country traditions of the Hudson valley
the western settlement and the backwoods narrative
the example of his friend the author of the burlesque American history
the republican party controversy of New York
the popular comedy of the national character
biographical_uncertainty: The division of the separate papers of the 1807 periodical between the three conductors has never been settled to general satisfaction, and the earlier state of the Dutch tale, as it existed before the recasting of 1831, is known only from its reprint and preface.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; essayist, tale-writer, sketch-writer, biographer and historian of the early republic, the central figure of the Knickerbocker group and the first American author of prose to obtain a wide British and European reputation
literary_identity: A writer of prose in several related modes: the comic antiquarian history, the periodical paper and character sketch, the legend and ghost tale of the Dutch country, the familiar essay of English scene and society, and later the romantic history and biography of the Spanish and American past. He wrote no poetry and no fiction of the systematic novel kind; his characteristic form is the sketch, in which observation, memory, humorous invention and moral reflection are left unwelded.
biography: He was born in New York City on 3 April 1783, the youngest but one of eleven children of a Scotch settling family, and was named, it was said, in honour of the recent declaration of independence. He was apprenticed to a law firm, was admitted to practice without ever taking much interest in the bar, and from about 1802 began to write for the New York papers with his brothers. In 1807 and 1808 he shared with his friend James Kirke Paulding the periodical Salmagundi, and in 1809 he brought out at New York the burlesque history which established the persona of Diedrich Knickerbocker. Business disaster in the family importing house sent him to England on its affairs from 1815 to 1823, and there he wrote the English and American sketches of The Sketch Book, issued in parts from 1819 to 1820 and making his name on both sides of the Atlantic. He published miscellaneous histories and sketches of the British and Spanish field through the middle 1820s, travelled in the American prairies in 1832, and in 1835 settled at Sunnyside on the Hudson, where he built up a reputation as the senior man of letters of the country. He served as United States minister at Madrid from 1842 to 1846, wrote the life of Washington in five volumes at Sunnyside, and died there on 28 November 1859, a few weeks after finishing the last volume.
literary_profile: His work falls into a humorous historical group, a group of essays and tales in the manner of the periodical sketch, and a late group of biography, history and travel; between them he compiled lives of western and Spanish personages and a great deal of occasional address and preface. The History of New York and the Salmagundi papers are the native and comic beginning; The Sketch Book, with its two companion collections of 1822 and 1824, is the characteristic body of his work and the source of the American short tale. His later prose is antiquarian and diplomatic in tone, and his Spanish histories and biographies of Columbus and of the conquerors of Granada belong to the romantic treatment of national past rather than to scholarly history.
stylistic_characteristics: A smooth, old-fashioned, consciously literary English, shaded from easy irony into sentiment without the reader being warned of the turn. He is an excellent describer of quiet scenery and of ruined places, a droll narrator in the personating vein, and a writer who prefers the half-light of the legend and the sketch to the resolved plot; his humour is generated by persona, by the assumption of a naive or pompous voice, and by the pedantic accumulation of invented authority.
intellectual_concerns: The making of an American literary past out of Dutch, Indian and revolutionary materials; the depreciation and the admiration of the old country by a colonial writer; the value of tradition, holiday and legend to a calculating republic; the commerce of the nations and the fate of the settled and displaced peoples of America; the education of taste through English scene and architecture; the dignity of the man of letters in a country of lawyers and merchants.
historical_significance: He gave the American short prose tale its first durable models and the sketch essay its American manner, and by his success with British publishers and readers he established that American writing could be a European commodity. Diedrich Knickerbocker named a school, a city's mythology and a literature's self-image, and The Sketch Book was the most widely read American book of its generation. His late life of Washington and his prairie travel also fixed the sentimental and legendary treatment of the national story for a century.
major_influences: The English periodical essay of Addison and Goldsmith
Sterne and the sentimental journey
the antiquarian humour of the English chroniclers
Scott's romantic prose fiction and his prefaces
Spanish ballad, chronicle and Moorish legend, which he read and translated
the Dutch and Indian traditions of the Hudson valley
the comic-chapter history of the schoolmaster and the local antiquarian
his own brothers' theatrical and journalistic circle in New York
biographical_uncertainty: The story of his naming in honour of the declaration of independence is family tradition rather than documented fact; the precise extent of Paulding's and of his brother's share in the Salmagundi papers has never been settled to general satisfaction.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, political editor, critic and translator, the first American poet of the nineteenth century to command an international audience and the founder of the American nature lyric in the Wordsworthian manner
literary_identity: A poet of short and middle-length meditative and descriptive pieces and of a few longer topographical poems, together with an enormous body of editorial, critical and political prose. His verse is predominantly blank verse and the didactic or descriptive stanza; his later work included the prose retelling of the Latin tale, a national poem of the Revolution's memory and the blank verse translation of Homer which completed his career. As editor of a New York daily for near half a century he was also a principal political writer of his time.
biography: He was born at Cummington, in the hill country of western Massachusetts, on 3 November 1794, the second son of Peter Bryant, a physician and occasional writer of the neighbourhood, and he learned his first Latin and Greek at his father's table. He went to Williams College in 1810 and left in the following year without a degree, then studied law, was admitted to the bar and for a short season practised in the same western counties. In 1811 he married his cousin Frances Fairchild, and about these same years he wrote the pieces which first made his name, including the brief satirical poem on national policy which he gave out under a disguise to spare his father's Federalist connections. His early meditative poem was printed in a Boston review in 1817 and was for long treated as the beginning of his reputation, and the volume of 1821 established him as a poet of the American scene. Finding no support for literature in Massachusetts, he removed to New York in 1825, took a share in the editing of periodicals, and from 1829 until his death was the leading spirit of a great daily newspaper, in which he wrote the political and literary argument of a generation of New York conservatives and reformers. He lectured on the national literature, edited a poetical and prose anthology, wrote the long poem on the American prairies at the end of his active work, and in the last years completed his blank verse Homer. He died in New York in June 1878, having been for half a century the most public of American men of letters.
literary_profile: His verse is small in bulk compared with his prose and is built around a few durable meditations, a group of short lyrics on waterfowl, flowers, death and the seasons, and two long descriptive poems of the prairie and of American history. His editorial and critical work fills an enormous file of newspaper columns and a course of lectures and addresses, and his translations, Latin fables, Homer and the prose romance retelling, occupy a large part of his later labour. The theory he held of poetry as moral and serious thought in elevated numbers gave the American nature lyric its first sustained practice, and he was the acknowledged centre of the New York literary world for thirty years.
stylistic_characteristics: A grave, sustained and deliberately elevated diction in blank verse of great smoothness, with long sentences, frequent inversion, apostrophe and a moral close; in the shorter lyrics a plain descriptive accuracy which passes into meditation. He is a poet of twilight, winter, water and the death of the year, and his strength is the slow descriptive paragraph in verse rather than the quick stroke of passion or the comic vein, which he rarely attempted.
intellectual_concerns: Death, immortality and the consoling proof drawn from the order of nature; the soul's instruction by landscape and solitude; the transience of earthly glory and the permanence of moral truth; the dignity and the destiny of the republic and of its western wilderness; the religion of a reasonableness hostile to sect and to fanaticism; the education of a nation's taste by criticism and by the daily press.
historical_significance: He fixed the American nature meditation in the blank verse and the diction of the English eighteenth century, and through a long editorial career he gave poetry and criticism a recognised place in American public life. His shortest poems entered the schoolbook and the recitation as no American verse had done, and his Homer remained for a generation the standard English rendering. As a political editor he also shaped the antislavery and reform opinion of the North, so that his literary and his public authority were exercised in one continuous career.
major_influences: The English meditative night and grave poetry of Young and of the graveyard school
Goldsmith and Thomson's descriptive blank verse
Wordsworth, from whom he took the subject of the humble outdoor meditation without the diction
the eighteenth-century couplet of his early satire
the Latin and Greek poetry which he read as a country boy
the Federalist and then reform politics of western Massachusetts
the Scottish rhetoric of the common schools
biographical_uncertainty: The first printing of his earliest printed poem, and the exact relation between the 1811 and later texts, are imperfectly documented; the long dispute over how much of the meditative poem was his own work and how far his father's papers have been counted in it remains only partially settled.
